alinaMoments.description: A professional portfolio and booking website for a family and newborn photographer, built solo with Next.js and TypeScript. The site is available in four languages via next-intl (German, English, Romanian, Italian) with locale-prefixed routing throughout, and integrates Cal.com for shoot bookings. A review system backed by Neon Postgres and Drizzle ORM lets clients submit testimonials, while Resend handles both the contact form and email notifications for new reviews. Caching runs through Vercel KV in production, with a file-based store as a local development fallback. Scroll-driven storytelling is powered by GSAP, Framer Motion, and Lenis smooth scrolling, creating an editorial, gallery-like browsing experience across the portfolio, services, and pricing sections. Styled with Tailwind CSS and deployed on Vercel.

chargeHub.description: A dashboard for electric vehicle charging infrastructure, still in active development. Built solo with Nuxt 4, Vue 3, and Vuetify, it already shows an interactive MapLibre GL station map next to a live status list backed by Pinia for state management. Chart.js analytics, tariff views, and Zod-validated forms are being built out next, with Playwright and axe-core in place for end-to-end and accessibility testing. It's live and usable today, but not feature-complete yet — a fuller write-up will follow once it is.

join.description: Built collaboratively in a 5-person team, Join is a real-time Kanban task management application developed with Angular and Firebase. The board delivers live task synchronization via Firebase Firestore, user authentication, drag-and-drop workflow management across status columns, and a full contact system with task assignment, priority levels, and due dates. A summary dashboard provides an at-a-glance view of task statistics and upcoming deadlines. Working across five developers required coordinating component ownership, aligning on shared service interfaces, and Git workflows that mirror professional Angular development environments. Fully responsive and deployed live.

elPolloLoco.description: A 2D jump-'n'-run built from scratch on the HTML5 Canvas 2D API — no game engine, no rendering library, zero runtime dependencies. Play as Pepe, a villager fighting off a flock of wild chickens across a parallax-scrolled desert: stomp enemies or throw collected salsa bottles, gather coins for extra lives, and take down the 200 HP Endboss, which runs its own walk → alert → attack → lunge state machine. The engine is class-based OOP on a shared DrawableObject → MovableObject inheritance chain, with custom gravity and jump physics and layered, per-interaction collision detection with damage cooldowns. A single requestAnimationFrame loop owned by the World advances the simulation in fixed 35 ms steps drawn from a delta-time accumulator, so gameplay stays frame-rate independent and a backgrounded tab can't burst-catch-up. A shared image pool decodes each sprite once and pre-warms it so the first frame never stalls on a cold decode; every interval and timeout is torn down deterministically on game over or restart, and a Play Again button rebuilds the world in place without a page reload. Audio effects play from a round-robin pool for zero restart latency, with a mute state persisted to localStorage. The pure game logic — collision boxes, jump validity, damage cooldowns, collectible pickup — is covered by a dependency-free node:test suite that loads the classic scripts into a node:vm sandbox, alongside a headless-Chromium smoke test (puppeteer-core) that presses Play and asserts the canvas actually paints with no console errors. Lint-clean against an ESLint 10 flat config, with JSDoc on every class and function. Deployed on Cloudflare Pages behind a strict Content-Security-Policy with no unsafe-inline, plus X-Frame-Options, Permissions-Policy, Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy and long-lived immutable asset caching. Fully responsive, with on-screen touch controls that appear automatically on touch devices and a rotate-to-landscape prompt in portrait.

pokedex.description: An offline-first Pokédex PWA built in two phases: first entirely in vanilla JavaScript — no frameworks, just native browser APIs — to understand the platform from the ground up. Then migrated to TypeScript strict mode and Vite, without changing a single function. The Service Worker uses Workbox with separate caches for API responses (7 days, 300 entries) and sprites (30 days, 600 entries). Keyboard accessibility follows WAI-ARIA guidelines: focus trap inside the modal, ESC to close, arrow key navigation, and focus restoration to the previously active element. The holographic shimmer effect replicates physical trading cards: mouse position tracked via mousemove, injected into CSS custom properties --x/--y, and rendered through mix-blend-mode: color-dodge. 251 Vitest unit tests, a Playwright E2E suite (functional, accessibility via axe WCAG 2.1 AA, visual regression, and mobile), and ESLint with typescript-eslint strict ensure the correctness of the migrated codebase.

birthdayReminder.description: Conceived, designed, and built entirely solo — from initial idea to production deployment. This full-stack cross-platform app is structured across every layer: Angular 19 with NgRx spanning five independent state slices, an offline-first approach where IndexedDB is the single source of truth, and real-time cloud sync with Firebase Firestore and Storage via a pending-changes queue. The app ships as both a PWA with SSR on Cloudflare Pages and a native Android app via Capacitor, with push notifications delivered through both service workers and the native API. Google Calendar integration with OAuth 2.0 supports one-way and two-way sync with recurring events, alongside a full data pipeline for JSON, CSV, and vCard import/export. Quality is validated through Karma unit tests, Cypress E2E and visual regression tests, and axe-core accessibility audits — with zero critical violations and full NVDA screen reader support.

todoApi.description: A 2-person team project where Mihaela owned the entire backend architecture from scratch. Built with Python 3.11, FastAPI 0.115, and SQLAlchemy 2.0, the API follows a strict four-layer architecture (Router → Service → Repository → Database) with Pydantic 2 for input validation and custom exception handling. Runs on SQLite locally and PostgreSQL in production, with ISO 8601 UTC timestamps and automatic schema creation on startup. A comprehensive test suite of 23 tests — 13 unit tests covering business logic and 10 integration tests — all pass against an in-memory SQLite database in under 0.2 seconds. Deployed live on Render with interactive Swagger/OpenAPI docs, paired with a React + TypeScript + Vite frontend.

caseStudyAlinaMoments.title: Alina Moments Photography
caseStudyAlinaMoments.subtitle: A full-stack website for a freelance photographer
caseStudyAlinaMoments.soloNote: Solo project: concept, development, production, and maintenance — from the first commit to the live deploy

intro.heading: Starting point
intro.body: Alina is a freelance photographer in Wolfsburg specializing in newborn, family, couple, and event photography. Before this project she had no website of her own — only an Instagram profile. The goal was a multilingual (DE/EN/RO/IT) professional website with online booking, a contact form, and a moderated review system — no CMS, no agency, no second developer on the team.
intro.body2: Every part of the stack — from the review database to the Content Security Policy to the CI pipeline and deployment — was designed, written, and shipped to production by a single person, held to the same bar a team would set for itself: a dedicated branch and pull request for every change, automated quality gates, end-to-end tests on every merge.

results.heading: Results — measured live today
results.performanceDetail: Desktop, measured against the production URL, same methodology as the CI gate: 40ms RTT, 10 Mbps, no CPU throttling
results.e2eTestsLabel: end-to-end tests in the CI pipeline (Playwright, 4 browser engines)
results.bundleSizeLabel: shared JS bundle (automated gate in CI)
results.methodologyNote: A methodology note that also appears in the original write-up: on a real mobile network with standard throttling, the performance score drops to 63–68/100 — that reflects the actual cost of high-resolution images on a photography website, not a measurement error. The CI pipeline (local build, same desktop preset) consistently logs 83–84/100 across multiple runs.

liveFeatures.heading: What's live in production
liveFeatures.body: Online booking through Cal.com (lazy-loaded only on first hover/focus, so third-party cookies aren't loaded unasked), a contact form with Zod validation and email delivery via Resend, page-specific OG images, sitemap/robots, a PWA manifest, native dark mode, and four languages with correct hreflang.

testimonial.heading: A real, published review
testimonial.quote: “A shoot at its finest: no stiff poses, just real laughter and real faces. The photos look like they're straight out of a reel, only better. Everything happened in a flash and the result is amazing. These aren't photos, they're real memories. Rating: 10/10”
testimonial.author: Giuseppe, birthday shoot
testimonial.flow: The full flow is real: the client submits a review through the public form → the system writes a row with status pending to Postgres (Neon) → a moderation email with an HMAC-signed link goes out (one-click approve/reject, no sensitive data in the token) → once approved, the review is published and the homepage is revalidated via revalidateTag. Tested live on June 1, 2026 with a real review, confirmed by the client. Current state of the database: 1 approved, 1 pending review — honestly still a small number, since the site has only been live for a few weeks, but the infrastructure is verified and production-ready.

engineering.heading: Engineering, not just design
engineering.item1Title: A “harmless” Node import broke the CSP on every page.
engineering.item1Body: lib/utils.ts imported Node's crypto.timingSafeEqual in the same file that exports cn() — the CSS class utility used by every client component. As a result, Next.js also bundled the vm-browserify polyfill (which uses eval() internally) into every browser bundle, violating the strict-dynamic CSP. Found through empirical bisection (progressively stubbing components and inspecting the compiled chunks), not by guessing. Fix: moved the function into a server-only module. Lighthouse Best Practices: 78 → 100 (CI).
engineering.item2Title: Rate limiting could be bypassed under concurrency.
engineering.item2Body: The rate limiter ran get and set as two separate steps (TOCTOU) — concurrent requests could slip past the limit before the counter updated. Fix: atomic kv.incr(), for both Vercel KV and the local dev fallback.
engineering.item3Body: Moderation tokens and admin secrets were compared with === across four different endpoints — theoretically vulnerable to timing attacks. Fix: a central timingSafeStringEqual(), used everywhere a secret is checked.
engineering.item4Title: Two parallel E2E runs were blocking each other.
engineering.item4Body: The concurrency gate in ci.yml compared github.ref (push event) against github.head_ref (pull request event) — two values that never match. Result: every commit triggered two simultaneous E2E runs on the same shared runners, with intermittent timeouts on WebKit (reproduced live: same commit, one run green in 9:42, the other red in 16:51, running at the same time). Fix: github.ref_name instead of github.ref. Verified: the duplicate run is now cancelled within 2 seconds.
engineering.item5Title: API routes were silently redirected under the locale prefix.
engineering.item5Body: The i18n middleware didn't exclude /api/* from its matcher: with localePrefix: "always", every call to /api/admin/reviews was silently redirected to /de/api/admin/reviews (which doesn't exist). Discovered by manually checking that an expected 401 status actually came from the app code and not from Vercel. Fix: explicitly excluded api from the next-intl matcher.

honestStatus.heading: Honest status, not a mockup
honestStatus.item1: Live since June 1, 2026 — no staging environment: public domain, real database, real transactional emails.
honestStatus.item2: No custom domain — a deliberate, confirmed decision by the client, not a technical limitation.
honestStatus.item3: Single-author repository — all 48 pull requests were opened by the same person, checked by the CI gate, and merged; no second person did code review.
honestStatus.item4: Review volume is still low — 1 approved, 1 in moderation: the site has only been live for a few weeks, so the flow is verified but not yet tested at scale.

caseStudyBfsgScanner.title: bfsg-scanner
caseStudyBfsgScanner.subtitle: An accessibility scanner for WCAG 2.1 AA / EN 301 549 / BFSG
caseStudyBfsgScanner.soloNote: Open-source side project: concept, architecture, implementation, tests, CI/CD, release, and documentation — single developer.
caseStudyBfsgScanner.period: 2026 — v0.1.0 published to npm on September 1, 2026

intro.heading: Context / problem
intro.body: Since June 28, 2025 the BFSG (Barrierefreiheitsstärkungsgesetz) has made digital accessibility a legal requirement in Germany for many B2C businesses: e-commerce, banking, bookings, ticketing. Anyone who builds or operates these sites has to be able to demonstrate conformance.
intro.body2: The existing tools (axe, Lighthouse) return rule IDs, not legal citations, and analyze one page at a time. bfsg-scanner scans a whole site and maps every finding to the EN 301 549 / BFSG clause it breaks, producing a citable compliance report in JSON, HTML, or PDF.

whatItDoes.heading: What it does
whatItDoes.item1: Discovers the site's pages — sitemap.xml first, then a breadth-first crawl that respects robots.txt, with a configurable page limit.
whatItDoes.item2: Analyzes every page in a real Chromium via Playwright + axe-core, with a concurrency pool, per-host rate limiting, and an identifiable User-Agent.
whatItDoes.item3: Maps each violation to its WCAG 2.1 success criterion and the corresponding EN 301 549 clause — and, via § 4 BFSG, to the statutory presumption of conformity.
whatItDoes.item4: Produces the report as report.json (versioned JSON Schema), report.html (DE/EN, self-contained file), and report.pdf (A4, to be archived as a record).
whatItDoes.item5: Exits with a non-zero code once violations reach a configurable severity threshold, so a CI pipeline can block a merge on accessibility.

results.heading: In numbers
results.pullRequestsLabel: merged pull requests, each with its own Architecture Decision Record
results.osLabel: operating systems in CI — Linux, Windows, macOS
results.exitCodesLabel: documented semantic exit codes, with a reasoned hierarchy so CI knows why it stopped
results.reportFormatsLabel: report formats, from the same run
results.provenanceLabel: provenance on npm via OIDC trusted publishing — no long-lived token in the release workflow
results.demoViolationsLabel: violations found on the W3C's deliberately inaccessible demo site
results.demoViolationsDetail: across 5 pages — 11 critical, 13 serious — each with its WCAG criterion and EN 301 549 clause, in a single PDF
results.mappingLabel: every finding mapped from its WCAG 2.1 criterion to the EN 301 549 / BFSG clause

highlights.heading: Technical highlights
highlights.item1Title: Published to npm with SLSA provenance.
highlights.item1Body: Released via OIDC trusted publishing — no long-lived token anywhere in the release workflow, and npm 2FA on the account.
highlights.item2Title: 28 small pull requests, each reviewed on its own.
highlights.item2Body: Every one carries an Architecture Decision Record explaining the choice it makes, and its own task checklist.
highlights.item3Title: 146 tests, CI on three operating systems.
highlights.item3Body: The Vitest suite runs on Linux, Windows, and macOS on every push.
highlights.item4Title: The output is a stable contract, not an ad-hoc format.
highlights.item4Body: A versioned JSON Schema describes report.json, guarded by anti-drift tests with ajv so the shape can't silently change.
highlights.item5Body: Documented with a reasoned hierarchy, so a pipeline can tell an accessibility failure apart from a crawl error or a usage mistake.
highlights.item6Body: docs/SCANNING-ETHICS.md — scan only sites you own or are authorized to test; rate limiting, robots.txt, and an identifiable User-Agent are on by default.

demoResult.heading: Demonstrated result
demoResult.body: Run against the W3C's deliberately inaccessible demo site → 24 violations across 5 pages (11 critical, 13 serious), each with its WCAG criterion and EN 301 549 clause, in a single PDF.

learned.heading: What I learned
learned.item1: Real release engineering: provenance, OIDC trusted publishing, npm 2FA, publish-on-tag.
learned.item2: Designing the output as a stable contract (versioned JSON Schema), not an ad-hoc format.
learned.item3: Controlled concurrency and scanning "netiquette" — rate limiting, robots.txt, an identifiable UA.
learned.item4: Translating legal requirements (BFSG → EN 301 549 → WCAG) into verifiable, tested logic.
